title: Money & Banking
subtitle: Open an account, pay for things and talk about saving — without doing the maths in your head

lessons.title: À la banque
lessons.description: Open an account, use a card and a cash machine, and handle deposits, withdrawals and transfers in French.

blocks.heading: Le compte et la carte
blocks.body: Un compte is an account and une carte bancaire is the bank card that goes with it. French banks distinguish un compte courant (a current / checking account, for everyday money) from un compte épargne (a savings account). The card you use every day is la carte bancaire — people say ma carte or ma CB in conversation, and they type un code secret, never a "PIN".

blocks.heading: Retirer, déposer, virer
blocks.body: Three verbs cover most bank operations. Retirer means to withdraw, déposer means to pay in or deposit, and faire un virement means to make a transfer. All three are regular, and they take de l'argent or a precise amount: retirer cinquante euros. The machine outside the bank is un distributeur automatique, often shortened to un distributeur.

blocks.heading: Espèces, billets et pièces
blocks.body: Cash has three useful words. L'argent liquide or les espèces both mean cash; en espèces is the set phrase you hear at the till. Notes are des billets and coins are des pièces, and one hundred centimes make one euro. Remember that l'argent is uncountable in French, exactly like "money" in English: never say des argents.

blocks.heading: Je voudrais — the polite way to ask a bank for anything
blocks.body: Je veux (I want) sounds blunt at a counter. Use je voudrais (I would like) instead, followed by a noun or an infinitive. J'aimerais works the same way and is slightly warmer. Both are conditional forms, and at A2 you only need the je and nous shapes: je voudrais, nous voudrions.

blocks.heading: Le, la, les — replacing the thing you are talking about
blocks.body: To avoid repeating a noun, replace it with a direct object pronoun: le (masculine), la (feminine), les (plural). The pronoun goes BEFORE the verb, not after it as in English. Before a vowel, le and la become l'. In the passé composé the pronoun goes before avoir, and the past participle agrees: je l'ai signée (la lettre).

blocks.tip: Ask yourself "the verb + what?". If the answer follows with no preposition, it is a direct object and takes le / la / les.

passages.title: Un rendez-vous à la banque
passages.french:
Lundi matin, Claire est allée à son agence bancaire pour ouvrir un compte courant.
Le conseiller lui a demandé une pièce d'identité et un justificatif de domicile.
Elle avait son passeport, mais elle avait oublié sa facture d'électricité à la maison.
Heureusement, elle a pu la montrer sur son téléphone.
Le conseiller a rempli le formulaire avec elle, puis Claire l'a signé.
« Votre carte bancaire arrivera dans une semaine », a-t-il expliqué.
« Et le chéquier ? » a demandé Claire.
« Le chéquier arrive plus tard, dans quinze jours environ. »
Claire a déposé deux cents euros en espèces sur son nouveau compte.
En sortant, elle a retiré vingt euros au distributeur automatique pour son déjeuner.
passages.english:
On Monday morning, Claire went to her bank branch to open a current account.
The adviser asked her for an identity document and proof of address.
She had her passport, but she had left her electricity bill at home.
Luckily, she was able to show it on her phone.
The adviser filled in the form with her, then Claire signed it.
"Your bank card will arrive in a week," he explained.
"And the chequebook?" asked Claire.
"The chequebook comes later, in about two weeks."
Claire paid two hundred euros in cash into her new account.
On her way out, she withdrew twenty euros at the cash machine for her lunch.

lessons.title: Payer et dépenser
lessons.description: Pay at the till, talk about your monthly budget, and use lui and leur to say who you are paying, lending or giving money to.

blocks.heading: Payer : comment et combien
blocks.body: Payer takes no preposition before the thing you buy: je paie le café. Use par carte, en espèces or par chèque for the method, and pour + person when you pay on someone's behalf. Note the spelling: je paie (or je paye), nous payons, j'ai payé. At the till you will also hear régler, a slightly more formal way of saying to settle up.

blocks.tip: Sans contact (contactless) works up to fifty euros in France; above that the terminal asks for votre code.

blocks.heading: Le budget du mois
blocks.body: Un budget is what you plan; une dépense is each thing you actually spend. The fixed monthly costs are le loyer (rent), les charges (utilities and building fees), les factures (bills) and les abonnements (subscriptions). Dépenser is to spend money — never use it for time, where French says passer du temps.

blocks.tip: Faire ses comptes means to go through your accounts — a very common Sunday-evening expression.

blocks.heading: Prêter, emprunter, devoir
blocks.body: These three trip everyone up. Prêter is to lend (the money leaves you), emprunter is to borrow (the money comes to you), and devoir is to owe. Prêter and devoir take à + person: je prête vingt euros à Marc. Emprunter takes à as well, meaning "from": j'emprunte vingt euros à Marc.

blocks.heading: Lui and leur — the person you give the money TO
blocks.body: When the person comes after à — je donne l'argent à Paul — replace à + person with an indirect object pronoun. There are only two new ones: lui for one person (he OR she, no gender difference) and leur for several. Like all object pronouns they sit before the verb. Note that leur here never takes an -s: je leur parle.

examples.french: Je donne l'argent à Paul. → Je lui donne l'argent.
examples.english: I give the money to Paul. → I give him the money.

examples.french: Je donne l'argent à Sophie. → Je lui donne l'argent.
examples.english: I give the money to Sophie. → I give her the money.

examples.french: Je prête cinquante euros à mes parents. → Je leur prête cinquante euros.
examples.english: I lend my parents fifty euros. → I lend them fifty euros.

examples.french: Tu leur as rendu l'argent ?
examples.english: Did you give them the money back?
examples.note: in the passé composé the pronoun goes before avoir

examples.french: Je vais lui envoyer un virement demain.
examples.english: I'm going to send him a transfer tomorrow.
examples.note: with two verbs, before the infinitive

examples.french: Ne leur prête pas d'argent !
examples.english: Don't lend them money!
examples.note: in a negative command the pronoun stays before the verb

blocks.tip: Careful: lui is also the stressed pronoun meaning "him" after a preposition (avec lui). Same word, different job — the position tells you which.

blocks.heading: The verbs that call for lui / leur
blocks.body: A short family of very useful verbs takes à + person: donner, prêter, rendre, devoir, payer, offrir, envoyer, demander, dire, téléphoner, expliquer, répondre. With all of them you use lui and leur, even where English has no "to". If you also need to replace the thing, the order is: me / te / nous / vous, then le / la / les, then lui / leur.

examples.french: J'ai téléphoné à la banque. → Je lui ai téléphoné.
examples.english: I phoned the bank. → I phoned them.

examples.french: Elle explique le budget à ses enfants. → Elle leur explique le budget.
examples.english: She explains the budget to her children. → She explains the budget to them.

examples.french: Je dois cent euros à mon frère. → Je lui dois cent euros.
examples.english: I owe my brother a hundred euros. → I owe him a hundred euros.

examples.french: Il m'a rendu la monnaie.
examples.english: He gave me my change back.
examples.note: me works for both direct and indirect

examples.french: Le magasin ne leur a pas répondu.
examples.english: The shop didn't answer them.

examples.french: Je le lui ai déjà payé.
examples.english: I've already paid him for it.
examples.note: le (the thing) comes before lui (the person)

blocks.tip: Quick test: if you can slot "to someone" into the English sentence, French wants lui or leur.

passages.title: Le budget de Karim
passages.french:
Karim gagne mille six cents euros par mois.
Chaque premier du mois, il paie son loyer : cinq cent cinquante euros, charges comprises.
Ensuite viennent les factures, l'abonnement de téléphone et les transports.
Il lui reste environ six cents euros pour les courses et les sorties.
« Le problème, ce sont les restaurants », dit-il en riant.
Le mois dernier, il a dépensé deux cents euros au restaurant avec ses collègues.
Il leur a même payé le dessert un soir, parce que c'était son anniversaire.
Maintenant, Karim note toutes ses dépenses dans une application.
Quand un ami lui demande de l'argent, il accepte, mais il note la somme.
« Je prête volontiers », explique-t-il, « mais je n'aime pas oublier. »
passages.english:
Karim earns one thousand six hundred euros a month.
On the first of every month he pays his rent: five hundred and fifty euros, utilities included.
Then come the bills, the phone subscription and transport.
He has about six hundred euros left for groceries and going out.
"The problem is restaurants," he says, laughing.
Last month he spent two hundred euros at restaurants with his colleagues.
He even paid for their dessert one evening, because it was his birthday.
Now Karim writes down all his spending in an app.
When a friend asks him for money, he says yes, but he notes the amount.
"I'm happy to lend," he explains, "but I don't like forgetting."

lessons.title: Économiser
lessons.description: Talk about saving money and good deals, and compare prices with plus, moins, aussi and the superlative.

blocks.heading: Économiser, épargner, mettre de côté
blocks.body: Économiser is the everyday verb for saving — money, water or electricity. Épargner is the bank's word, used for money you put aside on purpose. In conversation people also say mettre de l'argent de côté (to put money aside) and faire des économies (to save up). The money itself is des économies, always plural.

examples.french: J'économise pour un voyage au Canada.
examples.english: I'm saving up for a trip to Canada.

examples.french: Elle met cent euros de côté chaque mois.
examples.english: She puts a hundred euros aside every month.

examples.french: Nous faisons des économies depuis janvier.
examples.english: We've been saving since January.

examples.french: J'ai utilisé toutes mes économies.
examples.english: I used up all my savings.

examples.french: Son livret d'épargne rapporte peu.
examples.english: Her savings account earns very little.

examples.french: Économiser l'eau, c'est aussi économiser de l'argent.
examples.english: Saving water also means saving money.

blocks.tip: Un livret A is the classic French tax-free savings account — almost everyone opens one as a child.

blocks.heading: Bonnes affaires et prix
blocks.body: Une bonne affaire is a bargain. Twice a year France has les soldes, official sale periods with real discounts; the rest of the year shops run des promotions. Une réduction or une remise is the discount itself, often expressed as a percentage: moins vingt pour cent. Something cheap is bon marché or pas cher — never bas prix.

examples.english: I got a bargain in the sales.

examples.english: Prices have gone up a lot this year.

blocks.tip: Careful with un solde (masculine, an account balance) and les soldes (the sales). Same spelling, very different meaning.

blocks.heading: Comparer avant d'acheter
blocks.body: Comparing is how you talk about money. The pattern is plus / moins / aussi + adjective + que: ce modèle est moins cher que l'autre. For quantities you compare nouns instead: plus de, moins de, autant de + noun + que. The verb comparer takes à or avec: je compare les prix avec ceux d'Internet.

examples.french: Ce manteau est moins cher que l'autre.
examples.english: This coat is cheaper than the other one.

examples.french: Le train est plus cher que le bus, mais plus rapide.
examples.english: The train is more expensive than the bus, but faster.

examples.english: We have as many bills as last year.

examples.french: Je compare toujours les prix avant d'acheter.
examples.english: I always compare prices before buying.

blocks.tip: Bon has an irregular comparative: meilleur, not plus bon. For the adverb bien it is mieux: ce magasin marche mieux.

blocks.heading: Plus, moins, aussi — comparing two things
blocks.body: With an adjective the frame is plus / moins / aussi + adjective + que. The adjective still agrees with the first noun: cette veste est moins chère. With a noun, use de instead: plus de, moins de, autant de + noun + que. And with a verb, put the word after it: je dépense moins que toi.

examples.french: Le bus est moins cher que le train.
examples.english: The bus is cheaper than the train.

blocks.tip: Bon becomes meilleur, never plus bon: cette offre est meilleure. The adverb bien becomes mieux: je gère mieux mon budget.

blocks.heading: Le plus, le moins — the superlative
blocks.body: To say the most or the least, put le / la / les in front of plus or moins. If the adjective normally follows the noun, the article is repeated: le magasin le moins cher. For "in / of", French uses de: le moins cher de la ville. The irregulars stay irregular: le meilleur prix, le mieux.

examples.english: It's the cheapest shop in the area.

examples.english: This is where you eat best for ten euros.

blocks.tip: Watch the preposition: "the cheapest in Paris" is le moins cher DE Paris, never "à Paris".

passages.title: Deux façons d'économiser
passages.french:
Léa et Thomas partagent un appartement à Lyon et veulent partir en Grèce en juillet.
Léa met deux cents euros de côté dès qu'elle reçoit son salaire.
« Si je garde l'argent sur mon compte courant, je le dépense », explique-t-elle.
Thomas fait le contraire : il compare tous les prix avant d'acheter.
Il achète ses vêtements d'occasion et attend toujours les soldes.
Le mois dernier, il a trouvé un manteau à trente euros au lieu de quatre-vingts.
« C'était la meilleure affaire de l'année », dit-il, très fier.
Léa trouve que sa méthode à elle est plus simple et plus sûre.
Thomas répond qu'il dépense moins qu'elle sur les petites choses.
En fin de compte, ils ont presque la même somme sur leur livret A.
passages.english:
Léa and Thomas share a flat in Lyon and want to go to Greece in July.
Léa puts two hundred euros aside as soon as she gets her salary.
"If I keep the money in my current account, I spend it," she explains.
Thomas does the opposite: he compares every price before buying.
He buys his clothes second-hand and always waits for the sales.
Last month he found a coat for thirty euros instead of eighty.
"It was the best bargain of the year," he says, very proud.
Léa thinks her own method is simpler and safer.
Thomas replies that he spends less than she does on small things.
In the end, they have almost the same amount in their savings accounts.
